questions.q: According to the Indian Census, a worker is defined as a person who participates in any economically productive activity with or without compensation. Which of the following would be classified as a MAIN WORKER in the primary sector? (a) A student who helps on family farm during holidays (b) A full-time agricultural labourer working 180 days a year (c) A retired teacher doing kitchen gardening (d) A software engineer who grows vegetables on weekends.
questions.a: Correct answer: (b) A full-time agricultural labourer working 180 days a year. The Census defines a main worker as someone who worked for 183 days (6 months) or more in the reference year. Agricultural labour qualifies as primary sector work. Option (a) is a marginal worker (<183 days), (c) is not economically productive (kitchen garden for self-consumption), (d) is a main worker but in tertiary sector (software engineering). A wrong answer reveals confusion between main vs marginal worker thresholds and sectoral classification criteria.

questions.q: In 2011, India's workforce distribution was approximately: Primary 46%, Secondary 23%, Tertiary 31%. By 2021 (PLFS estimates), it shifted to Primary 42%, Secondary 25%, Tertiary 33%. A student claims: "The primary sector share fell by 4 percentage points, so 4% of the workforce moved directly into factories." Explain why this reasoning is geographically flawed.
questions.a: The reasoning is flawed because: (1) The 4% decline in primary share is a net change — some workers left agriculture, but new entrants joined the workforce; (2) Workers leaving primary sector do not move directly to secondary — most transition to informal tertiary (construction, retail, transport) due to skill mismatch; (3) Secondary sector's share rose only 2%, not 4%, confirming limited manufacturing absorption; (4) Population growth means absolute numbers in primary may not have fallen. A wrong answer reveals misunderstanding of net vs gross flows, the "missing middle" in India's structural transformation, and the role of the informal service sector as a labour sponge.

questions.q:
Using the data below for two Indian states (Census 2011), calculate the "Sectoral Diversification Index" (SDI) for each state using the formula: SDI = 1 - Σ(sector_share²). Which state has a more diversified occupational structure?
State A: Primary 62%, Secondary 18%, Tertiary 20%
State B: Primary 28%, Secondary 32%, Tertiary 40%
questions.a:
State A: SDI = 1 - (0.62² + 0.18² + 0.20²) = 1 - (0.3844 + 0.0324 + 0.04) = 1 - 0.4568 = 0.5432
State B: SDI = 1 - (0.28² + 0.32² + 0.40²) = 1 - (0.0784 + 0.1024 + 0.16) = 1 - 0.3408 = 0.6592
State B has higher SDI (0.659 > 0.543), indicating more diversified occupational structure. A wrong answer (e.g., choosing State A) reveals inability to apply the Herfindahl-Hirschman concentration logic to workforce distribution, or arithmetic errors in squaring percentages. It also shows failure to recognise that high primary concentration = low diversification.

questions.q: Compare the occupational structure of Kerala (Primary 17%, Secondary 25%, Tertiary 58%) and Chhattisgarh (Primary 65%, Secondary 18%, Tertiary 17%) using Census 2011 data. Identify THREE geographical factors — one physical, one historical, and one policy-related — that explain this divergence.
questions.a: Physical: Kerala's high population density (860/km²) and limited arable land push labour out of agriculture; Chhattisgarh's vast forested plateau (Bastar) and mineral-rich plains support primary livelihoods. Historical: Kerala's early missionary education, land reforms (1970s), and Gulf migration (1970s onward) created human capital and remittance-funded service economy; Chhattisgarh's tribal hinterland had limited colonial infrastructure investment. Policy: Kerala's decentralised planning (People's Plan Campaign) and high public spending on health/education expanded tertiary employment; Chhattisgarh's post-2000 statehood focused on mineral-based industrialisation (secondary) but weak service-sector policy. A wrong answer lists generic factors (e.g., "literacy") without linking to specific mechanisms or confuses correlation with causation.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "India's rising tertiary sector share (31% to 53% of GDP, 1990-2023) while workforce share grew only 20% to 33% proves the service sector is highly productive and creates high-value jobs." Use the concepts of "jobless growth," "informalisation," and "bailey's law" (services absorb low-skill labour) in your evaluation.
questions.a: The statement is misleading. Rising GDP share with stagnant employment share indicates HIGH productivity but LOW job creation — the hallmark of "jobless growth" driven by IT, finance, and professional services (high-skill, high-wage). Meanwhile, most new tertiary jobs are in LOW-productivity informal services (retail, transport, domestic work) — Bailey's Law: services act as a "sink" for surplus labour. The productivity gap within tertiary is extreme: IT services productivity is 10-15x that of informal retail. A wrong answer (agreeing with the statement) reveals confusion between sectoral averages and intra-sectoral distribution, ignorance of the informal-formal divide in services, and failure to distinguish labour productivity from total factor productivity.

questions.q: Design a 3-indicator dashboard for a District Magistrate to monitor occupational structure transition in a predominantly agrarian district (current: Primary 72%, Secondary 12%, Tertiary 16%). Indicators must be measurable annually from existing data sources (Census, PLFS, ASI, UDISE, PM-KISAN), capture both quantity and quality of transition, and flag "premature deindustrialisation" risk.
questions.a: Good dashboard: (1) "Manufacturing Employment Elasticity" = %Δ secondary workers / %Δ district GDP (source: PLFS + District GDP estimates) — flags if <0.1 (premature deindustrialisation); (2) "Formal Tertiary Share" = (regular wage/salaried tertiary workers) / (total tertiary workers) × 100 (source: PLFS) — captures quality, target >30%; (3) "Youth Non-Farm Entry Rate" = % of 15-29 yr new workers in secondary+tertiary (source: PLFS + PM-KISAN beneficiary age data) — tracks structural shift at entry level. Poor answer lists generic indicators (e.g., "literacy rate," "number of factories") without measurability, data source linkage, or diagnostic power for the specific risk.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Occupational structure refers to the distribution of a country's working population across different economic sectors — primary (extraction of natural resources: agriculture, mining, forestry, fishing), secondary (manufacturing, processing, construction), and tertiary (services: transport, trade, banking, education, health, ______) — expressed as percentages of the total workforce, and it serves as a key indicator of the level of economic development and structural transformation of an economy.
Fill in the blank: Look at your own neighbourhood: count how many families earn a living from farming, how many work in factories or ______, and how many are in teaching, banking, delivery, or IT.
What is Occupational structure? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Occupational structure refers to the distribution of a country's working population across different economic sectors — primary (extraction of natural resources: agriculture, mining, forestry, fishing), secondary (manufacturing, processing, construction), and tertiary (services: transport, trade, banking, education, health.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: You will notice most adults around you are in services — but travel ______ km to a village and the picture flips.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Occupational structure?
questions.a: Students equate "tertiary sector growth" with "development" and assume all service jobs are high-productivity.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can calculate sectoral workforce percentages from Census data, interpret shifts in occupational structure across Indian states using the Clark-Fisher hypothesis, and explain the discrepancy between sectoral share in employment versus GDP with reference to disguised unemployment in agriculture and the "jobless growth".
